This page goes with **Chapter 20, The Neapolitan Chord** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Neapolitan.html). Read each section there
first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It uses the Roman numerals of [Chapter 7](roman-numerals.qmd) and the
harmonic functions of [Chapter 9](progressions.qmd).

Every drill has **Settings**, and is also on the [Theory Drills](theory-drills.qmd) page. **▶ Hear it** plays the chord and then V.

**Typing it:** `N` in root position, `N6` in first inversion. The book writes N, not ♭II, but `♭II`, `bII` and `♭II6` are
accepted too. Other chords: `iv`, `iv6`, `IV6`, `ii6`, `ii°6` (type `o` for °).

## 20.1 The Neapolitan chord

The Neapolitan is the **♭II** chord: a **major triad** built on the 2nd degree of the scale lowered a half step. In C that is
**D♭–F–A♭**, in major and in minor alike. Classical analysis labels it **N** instead of ♭II. It is most often in **first inversion**,
with its 3rd (scale degree 4) in the bass, written **N6**. Since it is an altered ii chord, it has **pre-dominant** function: it goes
to V. The book points out how composers sometimes mark the moment with a change of texture, register or loudness.
[Read 20.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/NeapolitanIntroduction.html)

::: {.rn-quiz}
<figure><figcaption>Beethoven, Symphony No. 7, Op. 92, I (the book's Figure 20.1.1)</figcaption>
<iframe class="dr-yt" src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/-4788Tmz9Zo?start=747&end=764&rel=0" title="Beethoven, Symphony No. 7" loading="lazy" allowfullscreen></iframe></figure>
:::

To find it: go up a **minor 2nd** from the tonic, and build a **major** triad there. The root takes the next letter name up (D♭ in C,
not C♯). In a minor key only the root is outside the key signature; in a major key the 5th is too (A♭ in C major).

| Key | N | N6 (lowest first) | Lead-sheet symbol of N6 |
|---|---|---|---|
| C major or minor | D♭ F A♭ | F A♭ D♭ | D♭/F |
| A minor | B♭ D F | D F B♭ | B♭/D |
| G major or minor | A♭ C E♭ | C E♭ A♭ | A♭/C |
| C♯ minor | D F♯ A | F♯ A D | D/F♯ |

Start with the symbols. Given the numeral, which chord is it? (And back again.)

<div class="drill" data-ex="neapsym" data-settings="mode=both&most=3&inv=both&dir=find"></div>

Write the notes, lowest first:

<div class="drill" data-ex="neapwrite" data-settings="mode=both&most=3&inv=both"></div>

On the staff, followed by V. Read the bass to tell N from N6:

<div class="drill" data-ex="neap" data-settings="mode=both&most=4&inv=both&chords=n&clef=treble,bass"></div>

## 20.2 Examples of the Neapolitan chord

The book's examples. In the *Moonlight* Sonata (C♯ minor) the Neapolitan is a D major chord. The book suggests playing the passage
with another pre-dominant in its place, **iv** (F♯m) or **ii°6** (D♯°/F♯), and listening to the difference. For the *Raiders* theme
it suggests IV, iv or iiø65.
[Read 20.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ExamplesOfTheNeapolitanChord.html)

::: {.rn-quiz}

The same comparison by ear. Each question plays **i – ? – V – i** in four voices. The chord before V is N6, iv or ii°6. In this
drill all three have scale degree 4 in the bass, doubled, and the same inner voices; only the top note differs. Over N6 it is the
lowered 2nd, which falls to the leading tone. Listen for that darker top note.

<div class="drill" data-ex="neapear" data-settings="mode=minor&most=3&show=ear"></div>

## For teachers

- **Links with your settings:** open a drill's **Settings**, then **Copy a link with these settings**. Add `&lock=1` for a test, `&count=20` for a score.
- **Chords drilled:** N and N6 in major and minor keys. N64 is not drilled. A key whose Neapolitan would need a double flat (C♭, G♭, D♭ and
  A♭ major, and a♭ minor) is skipped. With **Chords: with other pre-dominants**, the naming drill also
  asks iv, iv6, ii°6 in minor and IV, IV6, ii, ii6 in major (ii° only in first inversion). The answer "N" is what the book uses;
  ♭II is accepted as the same answer.
- **Resolution:** the naming drill always shows and plays V after the chord, in root position, close position above the bass.
- **The ear drill's voicing** is this site's own, not the book's (the chapter does not discuss voice leading): bass on scale degree 4,
  doubled in the alto, ♭6 in the tenor, ♭2 on top falling to the leading tone (a diminished 3rd) as V comes in. iv and ii°6 keep the
  same bass, tenor and alto, so the top note is the only difference. Starting from i, the bass falls a 5th to scale degree 4 while
  the alto rises to the doubled 4; some teachers would call that contrary octaves.
- **Checked:** `node tests/lessons/neapolitan-drill.test.js` generates about ten thousand questions and checks each by its own
  arithmetic: the root is a minor 2nd above the tonic on the next letter name, the triad is major, N6 has scale degree 4 in the bass,
  no other drilled chord has the lowered 2nd, exactly one answer is accepted, and the drawn notes are the ones played.
- **Videos:** the clips use the book's YouTube links and start and end times. Each was checked against YouTube. The *Moonlight*
  Sonata clip the book uses is a performance by Alicia Keys (on an "MLG Highlights" channel); the Beethoven 7 clip is Iván Fischer and
  the Concertgebouw Orchestra.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
